title: FPC review of UK bank capital – summary of stakeholder evidence gathering event
summary: The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee published a summary of a March 2026 stakeholder event where views diverged on UK bank capital requirements—some arguing for maintained or increased capital buffers given macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty, while others pointed to stress test performance as evidence requirements could be reduced. Key themes included limited buffer usability due to MDA threshold concerns and board risk appetite, and debate over whether the leverage ratio operates as intended as a backstop or is becoming a binding constraint. Note: This document summarizes stakeholder views and does not represent Bank of England positions.
key_points: Stakeholder views split on capital calibration: some cited heightened macroeconomic uncertainty supporting maintained or higher capital benchmarks; others pointed to post-crisis reforms and stress test performance supporting reductions
Capital is not currently a constraint on credit supply for most sectors, though lower requirements might help some lenders focused on SME growth
MDA thresholds and board risk appetite limit buffer usability—banks maintain headroom above regulatory triggers and comparable capital levels to peers

The leverage ratio may be operating as a binding constraint for some lenders rather than a backstop, potentially reducing risk sensitivity and incentivizing low risk-weighted business like repo to non-banks
UK banks held smaller buffers above regulatory requirements than peers in jurisdictions with lower CCyB resting rates, implying markets expect UK banks could use ~120 bps more buffer in stress
Regulatory uncertainty exists around future Pillar 2a requirements, PRA buffers, and the supervisory reaction function after buffers are breached
why_it_matters: This summary captures the current policy debate on UK bank capital calibration ahead of a formal FPC decision. Market participants should note that buffer usability remains structurally constrained by MDA rules and board risk aversion—meaning even if capital requirements are reduced, banks may not immediately pass through to more lending. The leverage ratio debate has implications for which types of credit (repo vs. SME lending) receive capital allocation. Important caveat: This document presents stakeholder evidence, not official Bank of England policy positions.
market_structure_context: The document discusses UK banking regulatory architecture including: buffer usability mechanisms, MDA (Maximum Distributable Amount) threshold triggers, leverage ratio framework design, and interactions between Pillar 2A, O-SII buffers, and CCyB. Key structural observation: UK banks face potentially overlapping capital requirements on domestic exposures that may affect pricing of UK-focused lending. The MDA restriction point was highlighted as a structural barrier to buffer release in stress.
important_numbers: ~120 bps additional buffer usage expected for UK banks vs. other European banks in a stress scenario
